headline: Argo not considering capital raising given discount to NTA; instead neutralising DRP by buying shares on market

Instead, the more value-accretive approach is to effectively shrink the company and make it more valuable per share. The DRP is being neutralised by buying stock on market rather than issuing new shares. He contrasts this with externally managed LICs where fee structures create incentives to grow FUM regardless of shareholder outcomes.
quote: Uh no. With our discount, much more prudent for us to be not diluting the company and raising at a discount, um but to actually, you know, effectively shrink the company and make it uh more valuable per share. So, you know, we um at from time to time do share purchase plans and dividend reinvestment plans we do do. We offered one with the last dividend. Um but we're neutralizing that, so that means we're actually buying the stock on market to transfer to those shareholders who want to be in the DRP as opposed to issuing new stocks.

headline: Argo Investments acknowledges persistent share price discount to NTA and outlines steps being taken to close it, including buybacks and DRP neutralisation.
reasoning: Management acknowledges the share price discount to NTA is disappointing and continues to be a challenge, noting it has grown rather than reverted as expected. They attribute the discount primarily to dividend-related factors (level, franking, consistency of payments) and higher interest rates, as well as marketing and perception issues. To address this, Argo has neutralised three consecutive DRPs by buying shares on-market rather than issuing new shares, avoiding dilution. The company has also been active in buying back its own shares, viewing this as one of the better investments at current discount levels — equivalent to buying 85 cents in the dollar — with buybacks being accretive to earnings, capital value per share, and the franking balance.
quote: We've neutralized three DRPs in a row now, which means instead of issuing new shares, we're just buying them on market to redistribute to those that are in the DRP to satisfy their needs. Now, that avoids dilution. And we've also been, you know, relatively active in buying back our gas shares, cuz we think at this discount, that's actually one of the better investments we can make. And while you may say, 'Well, there's not a lot of impact. The share price discount hasn't closed.' I mean, that's probably not why we're buying back the stock. I mean, for us, it's like we're buying 85 cents in the dollar. And it's accretive to earnings, the capital value per share, the franking balance. So, it enhances the value of all of these metrics over the remaining shares.

headline: Argo argues its LIC structure delivers superior and growing dividend income versus index ETFs, with grossed-up yield now 20% above pre-COVID levels
reasoning: Argo compares its dividend track record against index ETFs over the COVID period and beyond. While Argo did modestly cut its dividend during COVID, it has since grown its dividend to a grossed-up yield 20% above the 2019 record of 33 cents per share. By contrast, the index ETF's dividend fell heavily during COVID as many Australian companies stopped paying, and despite a strong bounce-back, the ETF is currently paying less in absolute terms than it was in 2019 — before accounting for tax. Argo highlights the advantage of franking credits for investors who can utilise them, arguing the income maths favour the LIC structure for investors seeking a regular and growing income stream.
quote: And when we've mapped this, if we go back to pre-COVID, so we took at the time in 2019, Argo had paid a record high dividend of I think 33 cents per share. Now, we were a little cautious through COVID, so we did cut our dividend modestly. Um clearly, the governments threw money at the economies and and we've grown and grown ever since. So, now we're paying grossed up a yield that's 20% above where it was. If you look at the index ETF, you know, it fell heavily through COVID as a lot of companies in Australia, you know, stopped paying dividends, bounced back strongly, so sure had a couple of good years. It's currently paying a dividend that is less than what it was paying in 2019 in an absolute terms, and that's before the tax. So, if you're looking for a regular and growing income stream and can utilize the franking credits, we just think the maths on Argo or the traditional LIC and just speaks for itself.
episode_title: Argo vs ETFs: Lower Dividend Volatility

headline: Team Invest's Andrew Coleman is uninterested in Argo Investments LIC, arguing the 16-17% NTA discount is insufficient to justify paying for external fund management
reasoning: Coleman frames the LIC decision around two questions: whether the fund manager is better than the individual investor, and whether the NTA discount is large enough. For Team Invest members who manage their own wealth, neither question has a satisfying answer. A 16-17% discount to NTA is interesting but won't deliver 15-20% per annum returns. He prefers members to manage their own portfolios rather than pay someone to potentially underperform.
quote: If you're investing in an LIC, I assume you're doing so for one of two reasons... you're doing so because either you think that the managers of that LIC are wonderful fund managers and you'd like to be with them on their journey, or you think that they are trading at such a discount to NTA that you're happy to arbitrage that differential... a discount of 16, 17% to NTA is interesting, but it's not going to get you 15% or 20% per annum. So from that point of view, it wouldn't be one that our members are interested in.
